The United States House of Representatives. The lower chamber of Congress, established by the Constitution with 435 voting members apportioned among the states according to their population. Members serve two-year terms and function alongside the Senate as the legislative branch.

The House was designed to be far more directly responsive to the people than the Senate. This reflects the principle of direct popular sovereignty through proportional representation, even though the smallest states must have at least one representative. The number of representatives was fixed at 435 in 1913. While Congress could theoretically change this number, it has remained stable. Representation is reapportioned among the states every ten years following the decennial census.

The Speaker of the House is elected by members and holds the second position in the line of presidential succession, right after the Vice President. The Speaker's role combines legislative leadership with ceremonial authority. The House also has the power of the purse. All revenue bills must originate in the House—this is called the Origination Clause. The House controls federal appropriations, which gives it considerable power in budgetary disputes with the executive branch.

The House also holds the exclusive power of impeachment, bringing formal charges against federal officials, including the president. Once the House impeaches, the Senate then conducts the trial and votes on removal.

Major civil rights legislation of the nineteen sixties passed through the House after intense parliamentary struggles. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 are the most prominent examples. These victories were particularly significant because the House's composition reflected the regional and partisan divisions that made passing them a real achievement. Throughout its history, the House has included many figures who became national leaders or whose committee work advanced major policy initiatives. The House Judiciary Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee are particularly influential institutions. The House exemplifies the separation of powers and stands as a cornerstone of representative democracy in the United States.
